query: Current official France or European guideline for gestational trophoblastic disease oncology, including INCa, French reference centre, ESMO or ESGO, verify publication date and canonical URL
response:
## Bottom line

The **newest clearly dated European guideline** I could verify is the **2025 multidisciplinary practical guideline produced jointly by EOTTD, ESGO, GCIG and ISSTD**. Its journal issue publication date is **20 June 2025**. It is newer than both the **2020 EOTTD guideline** and the formal **2013 ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline**.  
[PubMed record, PMID 40359461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40359461/) · [ESGO evidence mentioning the complete citation](https://www.esgo.org/media/2026/01/Abreu_final.pdf)

### Verified sources

| Resource | Status and authority | Verified publication date | Canonical/stable URL |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **Practical Guidelines for the Treatment of Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Collaboration of the EOTTD–ESGO–GCIG–ISSTD** | **Current European multidisciplinary guideline.** ESGO is a named collaborating society; the document was published in *Journal of Clinical Oncology*. This is the newest dated European guidance identified. | **20 June 2025**, *JCO* 43(18):2119–2128 | [PubMed PMID 40359461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40359461/) |
| **ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease** | Official ESMO guideline landing page. ESMO continues to list GTD among its gynaecological cancer guidelines, but the underlying identifiable CPG is the 2013 publication below. | Landing page itself does not expose a reliable publication/update date in the indexed content | [Official ESMO GTD page](https://www.esmo.org/guidelines/esmo-clinical-practice-guideline-gestational-trophoblastic-disease) · [ESMO gynaecological-guidelines index](https://www.esmo.org/guidelines/guidelines-by-topic/esmo-clinical-practice-guidelines-gynaecological-cancers) |
| **Gestational trophoblastic disease: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up** | Formal, peer-reviewed ESMO CPG by Seckl et al. It remains authoritative historically but is substantially older than the 2025 ESGO collaboration. | **October 2013**, *Annals of Oncology* 24 Suppl 6:vi39–vi50 | [Publisher full text](https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534%2819%2931565-0/fulltext) · [DOI: 10.1093/annonc/mdt345](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdt345) |
| **Practical clinical guidelines of the EOTTD for treatment and referral of gestational trophoblastic disease** | Earlier European harmonisation guideline from EOTTD; useful background but superseded chronologically by the 2025 EOTTD–ESGO–GCIG–ISSTD document. | **2020**, *European Journal of Cancer* | [Publisher record, PII S0959804920300629](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959804920300629) |
| **Centre de Référence des Maladies Trophoblastiques, Lyon** | Official French specialist reference-centre resource providing registration, expert review and French management information. It is an institutional reference resource, not automatically an INCa-labelled national clinical-practice guideline. | No reliable publication/update date was visible for the centre’s general online material; individual protocols should therefore be checked for dates on the documents themselves | [French reference-centre website](https://www.mole-chorio.com/) |

## France/INCa finding

I did **not** identify a current, separately published and clearly dated **INCa clinical-practice guideline specifically for gestational trophoblastic disease**. INCa’s role in organising French rare-cancer referral networks should not be confused with authorship of every protocol issued by a designated expert centre. Accordingly, the Lyon reference-centre material should be cited as **French expert-centre guidance**, unless an individual document explicitly carries INCa endorsement or methodology.  
[INCa official site](https://www.e-cancer.fr/) · [French reference centre](https://www.mole-chorio.com/)

## Recommended citation for current practice

For a protocol, evidence review or clinical decision document, the best current European citation is:

> **Practical Guidelines for the Treatment of Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Collaboration of the European Organisation for the Treatment of Trophoblastic Disease–European Society of Gynaecologic Oncology–Gynecologic Cancer InterGroup–International Society for the Study of Trophoblastic Diseases.** *Journal of Clinical Oncology*. 2025;43(18):2119–2128. Published 20 June 2025. [PubMed PMID 40359461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40359461/).

The **2013 ESMO CPG** should be identified by its actual date rather than described as a newly updated ESMO guideline. The **2025 document is ESGO-collaborative, not an ESMO-branded CPG**.

citations.snippet:
Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. Since GTD and its malignant sequel gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) are rare diseases , little evidence is available from randomised controlled trials on optimal treatment and follow-up. Treatment protocols vary within Europe, and even between different centres within countries. One of the goals of the ‘European Organisation for Treatment of Trophoblastic Diseases’ (EOTTD) is to harmonise treatment in Europe. To provide a basis for European standardisation of definitions, treatment and follow-up protocols in GTD, we composed a set of guidelines for minimal requirements and optimal management of GTD.

citations.snippet:
Only 1 out of 17 high-risk patients developed drug resistance, and 3 needed urgent surgery. The relapse rate of responders was 19% after a median of 5.5 months. The survival rate of high-risk patients was 88%, of which 76% are alive with no evidence of disease, while 12% have still detectable beta-chorionic gonadotrophin. The remission rate in the second-line treatment group was 64%, higher than using other regimens such as MAC or CHAMOCA. In conclusion, we consider EMA/CO to be the best choice for patients with high-risk GTT, because it is effective and well tolerated. EMA/CO regimen in high-risk gestational trophoblastic tumor (GTT)

Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. Since GTD and its malignant sequel gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) are rare diseases , little evidence is available from randomised controlled trials on optimal treatment and follow-up. Treatment protocols vary within Europe, and even between different centres within countries. One of the goals of the ‘European Organisation for Treatment of Trophoblastic Diseases’ (EOTTD) is to harmonise treatment in Europe. To provide a basis for European standardisation of definitions, treatment and follow-up protocols in GTD, we composed a set of guidelines for minimal requirements and optimal management of GTD.

sources.snippet:
Only 1 out of 17 high-risk patients developed drug resistance, and 3 needed urgent surgery. The relapse rate of responders was 19% after a median of 5.5 months. The survival rate of high-risk patients was 88%, of which 76% are alive with no evidence of disease, while 12% have still detectable beta-chorionic gonadotrophin. The remission rate in the second-line treatment group was 64%, higher than using other regimens such as MAC or CHAMOCA. In conclusion, we consider EMA/CO to be the best choice for patients with high-risk GTT, because it is effective and well tolerated. EMA/CO regimen in high-risk gestational trophoblastic tumor (GTT)

The corresponding official society entry is on the [ESMO uveal-melanoma guideline page](https://www.esmo.org/guidelines/guidelines-by-topic/melanoma-and-other-skin-cancers/uveal-melanoma).

I did **not** find evidence of a single current France/Europe guideline covering all “ophthalmic and orbital tumours.” Guidance remains divided by histology—uveal melanoma, retinoblastoma, lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, lacrimal/salivary-type carcinoma, sinonasal tumour invading the orbit—and by age group.

## Source assessment

| Organisation/source | What can be verified | Date and canonical URL | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ESMO** | *Uveal melanoma: ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up*. It is the clearest current European guideline addressing definitive ocular radiotherapy. | Published online **17 July 2023**. [Canonical DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annonc.2023.06.016); [official ESMO page](https://www.esmo.org/guidelines/guidelines-by-topic/melanoma-and-other-skin-cancers/uveal-melanoma). | **Primary authoritative guideline** |
| **SFRO** | SFRO publishes its national radiotherapy recommendations as the **RecoRad** series in *Cancer/Radiothérapie*. The currently indexed general update is the **2022 RecoRad edition**, but I could not verify a stable article-level canonical URL for a dedicated eye-and-orbit chapter from the accessible evidence. The publisher identifies the 2022 papers as updates of SFRO recommendations ([publisher record/example](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1278321821002699)). | **2022** corpus; individual eye/orbit citation requires confirmation in the journal issue or SFRO catalogue before use. | **Primary society corpus, but dedicated ophthalmic chapter not sufficiently verified here** |
| **Institut Curie** | Institut Curie is a major French ocular-oncology and proton-therapy provider. Its institutional material describes treatment/services, but an institutional treatment page is **not itself a national or European clinical-practice guideline**. | [Institut Curie institutional site](https://institut-curie.org/). Page-level publication/revision dates should be checked individually because many service pages do not expose a formal guideline version date. | **Primary institutional information; not a guideline** |
| **ESTRO** | I found no verified, dedicated ESTRO/ACROP guideline covering ocular or orbital tumours as a single entity. ESTRO guidance may apply indirectly—for example, paediatric radiotherapy, lymphoma, sarcoma or head-and-neck target delineation—but should not be represented as an ocular-tumour guideline. | [Official ESTRO website](https://www.estro.org/). | **No dedicated guideline verified** |
| **EURACAN** | No stand-alone EURACAN “ophthalmic and orbital tumours radiotherapy” guideline was verified. Relevant EURACAN/ESMO documents may instead be organised under rare head-and-neck cancer, melanoma, sarcoma or salivary/lacrimal-type malignancy. | [Official EURACAN site](https://euracan.eu/). | **No umbrella orbital-radiotherapy guideline verified** |
| **SIOPE** | Retinoblastoma and orbital rhabdomyosarcoma belong in paediatric European pathways, but I did not verify a current SIOPE document functioning as a comprehensive ophthalmic/orbital radiotherapy guideline. SIOPE standards should be checked by disease because contemporary retinoblastoma management generally treats radiotherapy as a selected rather than universal modality. | [SIOPE European Standard Clinical Practice programme](https://siope.eu/activities/european-standard-clinical-practice/). | **Disease-specific paediatric material; no umbrella guideline verified** |

## Older documents that should not automatically be called “current”

An older ESMO retinoblastoma guideline exists:

- **“Retinoblastoma: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up,” 2013**, [doi:10.1093/annonc/mdt163](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdt163).

Because it was published in **2013**, it should not be presented as the current European radiotherapy standard without confirmation that ESMO or SIOPE still formally lists it as active and without comparison against newer paediatric retinoblastoma protocols.

## Practical citation recommendation

For a contemporary protocol, policy or literature review:

1. Cite the **2023 ESMO uveal-melanoma guideline** as the principal verified European source for ocular melanoma radiotherapy.
2. For French technical practice, retrieve the relevant **SFRO RecoRad 2022 article directly from the SFRO catalogue or the 2022 *Cancer/Radiothérapie* special issue** and record its DOI before citation.
3. Cite Institut Curie pages only as **institutional practice/service information**, not as national guidance.
4. For orbital lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, lacrimal-gland carcinoma or sinonasal disease invading the orbit, use the corresponding **histology-specific lymphoma, paediatric sarcoma, salivary-gland or head-and-neck guideline**, rather than extrapolating from the uveal-melanoma document.

**Evidence hierarchy used:** official society guideline and guideline publication = primary authoritative source; official institutional page = primary institutional information but not consensus guidance; PubMed/publisher indexing records = bibliographic verification rather than independent clinical guidance.

query: Current official Europe or international consensus guideline for radiotherapy of benign diseases, including DEGRO, ESTRO, RCR or ASTRO, verify publication date and canonical URL
response:
## Bottom line

The most current broad, directly verifiable European guidance is the **Royal College of Radiologists (RCR), _Recommendations for using radiotherapy for benign disease in the UK_**, published **March 2023**. It is an official national professional-society recommendation, not a Europe-wide consensus guideline.[1]

A newer **ASTRO–ESTRO–DEGRO–RANZCR** document, _Radiation Therapy for Nonmalignant Diseases: An ASTRO-ESTRO-DEGRO-RANZCR Framework_, is available from the journal publisher as a **2025 framework**. It is the best match for an international multisociety consensus, but it is explicitly styled a **“framework,” not a formal clinical-practice guideline**.[2]

### Authoritative documents

| Document | Status and scope | Verified publication date | Canonical/authoritative URL |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **Radiation Therapy for Nonmalignant Diseases: An ASTRO-ESTRO-DEGRO-RANZCR Framework** | International multisociety framework involving ASTRO, ESTRO, DEGRO and RANZCR. It is broader geographically than the national DEGRO and RCR documents, but should not be relabelled as a formal CPG when the authors call it a framework.[2] | **2025**. The publisher record establishes the year; I could not independently verify an exact online-publication day from the accessible record, so no day is asserted. | [International Journal of Radiation Oncology • Biology • Physics / Red Journal](https://www.redjournal.org/article/S0360-3016(25)06299-6/abstract) |
| **RCR: Recommendations for using radiotherapy for benign disease in the UK** | Current official UK recommendations covering selection, justification, consent, governance and clinical use of radiotherapy for benign disease.[1] | **March 2023**, printed on the official document.[1] | [Official RCR PDF](https://www.rcr.ac.uk/media/1trgbgsb/rcr-publications_recommendations-for-using-radiotherapy-for-benign-disease-in-the-uk_march-2023.pdf) |
| **DEGRO practical guidelines for radiotherapy of non-malignant disorders, Parts I–III** | German DEGRO/German Cooperative Group evidence-based guideline series addressing principles and risk, painful degenerative skeletal disorders, and hyperproliferative disorders. These remain important primary guideline publications but date from **2014–2015**, so they should not automatically be described as the newest international guidance.[3–6] | Part II was published online **20 September 2014** and in the **2015** journal volume; Parts I and III were published in **2015**.[3–6] | [Part I—PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26117368/); [Part II—publisher DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00066-014-0757-4); [Part III bibliographic citation](https://www.appliedradiationoncology.com/articles/radiation-therapy-in-the-treatment-of-plantar-fibromatosis-two-clinical-cases-of-recurrent-disease) |

## Important distinctions

- **RCR 2023 is the clearest current, fully accessible official clinical recommendation document**, but it is a **UK national** document rather than a European consensus.[1]
- **The 2025 ASTRO–ESTRO–DEGRO–RANZCR publication is the newest international multisociety document located**, but its formal designation is **framework**.[2]
- The Red Journal framework cites a **DEGRO benign-disease update from 2022**, but the accessible publisher record provides that item only as a reference and does not supply a verifiable public DEGRO canonical URL. I therefore would not substitute an unverified third-party copy for an official link.[2]
- I found **no comparably broad standalone ESTRO-only or ASTRO-only clinical-practice guideline** for all benign/nonmalignant diseases in the retrieved authoritative records; their broad current participation is through the joint framework.[2]
- PubMed and third-party journal pages are useful **secondary bibliographic records**. The RCR-hosted PDF, Red Journal article page, and DOI publisher pages are the **primary/canonical sources**.[1–3]

## Recommended citation hierarchy

1. For a **current international position**: cite the **2025 ASTRO–ESTRO–DEGRO–RANZCR framework**, while preserving the word “framework.”[2]
2. For an **implementable current European national recommendation**: cite **RCR 2023**.[1]
3. For disease-specific German dose/fractionation evidence and historical DEGRO recommendations: cite the applicable **DEGRO 2014–2015 part**, while checking whether a later disease-specific update applies.[3–6]

### Sources

1. Royal College of Radiologists. _Recommendations for using radiotherapy for benign disease in the UK_. March 2023. [Official PDF](https://www.rcr.ac.uk/media/1trgbgsb/rcr-publications_recommendations-for-using-radiotherapy-for-benign-disease-in-the-uk_march-2023.pdf).  
2. _Radiation Therapy for Nonmalignant Diseases: An ASTRO-ESTRO-DEGRO-RANZCR Framework_. International Journal of Radiation Oncology • Biology • Physics, 2025. [Publisher record](https://www.redjournal.org/article/S0360-3016(25)06299-6/abstract).  
3. Reichl B, et al. _DEGRO practical guidelines for radiotherapy of non-malignant disorders. Part I: physical principles, radiobiological mechanisms, and radiogenic risk_. 2015. [PubMed PMID 26117368](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26117368/).  
4. Ott OJ, et al. _DEGRO guidelines for the radiotherapy of non-malignant disorders. Part II: Painful degenerative skeletal disorders_. Published online 20 September 2014; journal volume 2015. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00066-014-0757-4).  
5. FAU research record for Part II, identifying it as a 2015 journal publication. [Institutional bibliographic record](https://cris.fau.de/publications/122075404).  
6. Seegenschmiedt MH, et al. _DEGRO guidelines for radiotherapy of non-malignant disorders. Part III: hyperproliferative disorders_. Strahlenther Onkol. 2015;191:541–548, as cited in the linked literature record.[Applied Radiation Oncology reference list](https://www.appliedradiationoncology.com/articles/radiation-therapy-in-the-treatment-of-plantar-fibromatosis-two-clinical-cases-of-recurrent-disease).
